vignette: Arjun sits on the edge of the padded chair, thumbs pressing into his palms as he describes the pediatric ICU. The memory arrives in precise, unyielding frames. His daughter, Maya, is four years old when a bacterial infection drops her from a healthy sprint to a ventilator bed. He remembers the sharp scent of chlorhexidine, the way the ceiling tiles blur under his tired gaze, and the rhythmic, mechanical breaths of the monitor that seem to dictate the pace of the room. When the attending physician uses the word critical, Arjun stops speaking. He learns to anchor himself in the small, steady rise and fall of her chest, memorizing the cadence of her survival. He holds her mother’s hand across the narrow bed, watching their daughter’s eyelids flutter, counting the seconds between heartbeats until the word stable finally breaks the silence. In the weeks that follow, Maya’s body recovers. The discharge summaries pile on the kitchen counter like winter snow. But Arjun does not step back into his old life. He is fifty now, a freelance animator who spends his days coaxing stillness into motion. Before Maya’s illness, his workflow felt instinctive. He would sketch character arcs, plot keyframes, and watch lines transform into fluid gestures on his tablet. Now, the software feels like a locked door. When he opens the timeline, his cursor freezes. The horizontal bars trigger a familiar contraction in his sternum, a phantom echo of those hospital monitors. He tells me he cannot commit to a sequence because the forward progress of animation feels like surrendering control. He sets the tablet aside and stares at the blank canvas until the tension in his shoulders releases. His days are built around quiet containment. He wakes at 3:47 a.m., the exact hour the night nurse once called with Maya’s dropping oxygen saturation. He lies rigid until his heart rate slows, then rises to check the deadbolts, the stove valves, the smoke detector batteries. He cannot sleep through the deep stages of the night because he equates heavy rest with the absence of vigilance. When Maya calls from her university dorm, his shoulders drop a fraction, but he cannot process her casual tone. He replays childhood fevers in his mind, scanning for overlooked symptoms, wondering if a delayed reaction might resurface. He answers politely, then flips his phone face-down on the desk. His wife, Priya, notes the growing distance. She says he startles at sudden noises, at car backfires, at the news anchor mentioning a pediatric ward outbreak. He apologizes for the flinch, but the reaction lives in his nervous system long before his mind catches up. He stops attending extended family gatherings because the sound of children running up wooden stairs feels like a threat. South Asian hospitality once meant his home hummed with relatives, clattering dishes, and overlapping conversations. Now, he keeps the blinds lowered, the television muted, the apartment quiet enough to hear his own pulse. At his desk, Arjun attempts to work. He draws a boy mid-leap, then erases him. He sketches a clock, then scratches the face with his stylus. He explains that animation requires faith in the future—the guarantee that frame thirty-two will follow frame thirty-one. Lately, he can only render the immediate present, frozen and unyielding. His clients have noticed the delays. He misses deadlines not out of indifference, but because he sits in his chair, watching the cursor blink, waiting for the ground to stop shifting. When I ask what the waiting feels like, he says it feels like holding his breath in a room where the air keeps thinning. He exhales only when the house is still. He still loves Maya. He still loves Priya. He still mourns the man who used to wake to the sun instead of the alarm. But the world now moves in sudden jolts, and he braces for every shift. His hands rest on the desk, steady, but his mind remains in that room, counting the lights, counting the seconds, counting the reasons to stay awake.
